newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Makers of Indonesia's national car to build vans.
newsitem.headline: Makers of Indonesia's national car to build vans.

text.p: The makers of Indonesia's controversial "national car" said on Tuesday they also plan to manufacture utility vans with probably the same tax-free privileges that have drawn fire from the U.S., the European Union and Japan.

PT Timor Putra Nasional spokesman Mohamad Ircham confirmed the company plans to make utility vans with Kia Motors Corp, its partner in the national-car project, once their local production facility is operational around May 1998.
"Yes, we do have such a plan and I think it will be included (in the national car programme)," Ircham told Reuters.
A Kia Motors official said on Tuesday in Seoul that plans called for the manufacture of 50,000 utility vans a year in Indonesia beginning in 1998.

"After discussions with our joint-venture partner PT Timor Putra Nasional and the Indonesian government, we have agreed on a plan to include production of utility vans in Indonesia's national-car project," Kia's executive vice president Kim Seung-ahn said.

"The production capacity of the national-car plant, which is scheduled to have an annual capacity of 70,000 vehicles, could rise to 120,000 if we go ahead with the plan to make vans," said Kim. "The plant is scheduled for completion by early 1998."
Kia and PT Timor Putra Nasional, which is controlled by President Suharto's son Hutomo Mandala Putra, officially launched Indonesia's national passenger car, dubbed the "Timor", on October 1.
The four-door 1,600-cc sedan is currently made in South Korea and exported to Indonesia, but will eventually be manufactured in Indonesia.
The car has a three-year exemption from excise and luxury taxes as long as it meets local-content requirements.

Japan, the U.S., and the EU have all complained to the World Trade Organisation, arguing that the policy discriminates against existing automobile joint ventures in Indonesia. Most of them are with Japanese firms.

"If they make the van under the same conditions as the Timor car, its hard to imagine the Europeans having a different attitude. They would object on the same grounds," one European official told Reuters.
Informed sources said the U.S. and Japan are expected to raise similar objections.
Ircham said the plan to build the van was part of PT Timor's broad strategy for entering the vehicle manufacturing sector.
"As well as the van, we have plans to make trucks, buses, jeeps and other vehicles," Ircham said.
"We have not yet decided whether to launch the vehicles with Kia or others and it is also not sure when we will launch them," he said.
